column4: The source section's dictionary note calls evzār the weapons of war; 47:4 says “ḥattā taḍaʿa al-ḥarbu awzārahā,” until war itself lays them down. The shift from war's gear to the addressee's removed burden makes the release audible as war's ending.

The source section cites “an taḍaʿū aslihatakum”: during the fear-prayer, rain or illness can permit setting arms aside while precautions remain. Here the weapon is put down temporarily within active danger, unlike the section's imagined end of war.

The source section explicitly cites “al-āna khaffafa Allāhu ʿankum,” God's easing of the military demand after the prior verse's ten-to-one ratio. This is a direct wartime counterpart to the load removed from a fighter.

At the battle with Jalut, the fighters ask “afriġ ʿalaynā ṣabran” and for firm feet and help. The source section's root note gives pouring as a sense of f-r-ġ; here what is poured into the combatants is patience.

The next ayah says “fa-hazamūhum bi-idhn Allāh”: Jalut's force is defeated and David kills Jalut. It supplies the battle's outcome after 2:250's plea for help and illuminates the source section's dictionary sense of w-z-r as overcoming.
God teaches David to make coats of armor “lituhṣinakum min ba'sikum,” to protect you from your violence. The armor worn and later laid down in the source section has this explicit defensive purpose.

Among God's protections are “sarābīla taqīkum ba'sakum,” garments that guard you in battle. This names the same protective clothing function as the source section's armor, which is carried through conflict and set down when it ends.
David is told to make full coats of mail and measure the links. That is a concrete instance of the armor in the source section's image, down to the linked construction of battle gear.

The source section's root note says ẓ-h-r can mean prevailing; 9:33 uses “li-yuẓhirahu ʿalā al-dīni kullihi,” to make the religion prevail over all religion. This is the specific Qur'anic use of victory named in the section.

The source section's dictionary note treats wizr as war gear borne on a back; 6:31 says the deniers carry their “awzārahum ʿalā ẓuhūrihim.” The same burden-and-back image is reversed: their loads remain on them at judgment rather than being removed.

The source section's dictionary note glosses f-r-ġ in “zehebe damuhu farghan” as blood going unclaimed. For an unjustly slain person, 17:33 grants the heir authority but forbids excess in killing, setting a limit on whether blood is left without redress.

The source section's dictionary form for f-r-ġ describes blood that goes unclaimed; 4:92 requires blood-money to be delivered to the slain person's family for accidental killing, unless they waive it. The verse gives a concrete legal opposite to blood left without claim.

“Al-qiṣāṣu fī al-qatlā” prescribes retribution in cases of the slain, while allowing pardon and payment. This gives legal shape to the source section's dictionary image of blood whose claim may or may not be pursued.

The ayah says not to weaken in pursuing the enemy, since they suffer too and believers hope in God. In the same war-prayer passage, it marks the active struggle that must continue before the source section's arms can be laid down at war's end.

This ayah commands fighting until persecution ends and religion belongs wholly to God, then says to stop if the other side desists. It gives a specific condition for the cessation that the source section pictures as war laying down its burdens.

The parallel command says to fight until fitna ends and, if the other side desists, cease aggression. This repeated boundary clarifies when the source section's end-of-war laying down of arms can occur.

“If they incline to peace, incline to it” sets a clear boundary for armed conflict. The source section pictures the moment war drops its gear; this ayah describes the decision to turn from fighting toward peace.

After the conquest at Mecca, God says He restrained both sides' hands from each other. The image of hands held back gives a concrete boundary to the armed scene in which the source section imagines weapons finally being set down.

This ayah gives the Torah rule “al-nafsa bi-al-nafs” and permits relinquishing the claim as charity. It is another specific legal account of a slain person's blood being pursued or waived, matching the source section's f-r-ġ dictionary sense.

The source section's root note connects ẓ-h-r with the back and prevailing; here the unbeliever is “ʿalā rabbihi ẓahīran,” a supporter against his Lord. That reversed direction sharpens the source section's insistence that the renewed stance is toward the Lord.

When called to fight, some “iththāqaltum ilā al-arḍ,” grow heavy and cling to the earth; the passage contrasts this with seeking the nearer life. It reverses the source section's fighter who bears gear through battle and lays it down only after the conflict.

This ayah commands the Prophet to urge the believers to fight and states the initial one-to-ten endurance ratio. The next ayah, 8:66, lightens that military burden; this verse supplies the demand that is eased.
God softens iron for David; the next ayah, 34:11, specifies that it becomes coats of mail. The metal-working scene supplies the material step behind the armor named in the source section.

This ayah permits shortening prayer while traveling if attack by disbelievers is feared. It establishes the danger around the next verse's armed prayer, where setting weapons down is only a temporary allowance.

After the fear-prayer, this ayah tells believers to remember God standing, sitting, or lying down, and to pray normally when safe. It continues 4:102's armed prayer and makes the transition from combat vigilance to devotion explicit.

The source section's dictionary note links ẓ-h-r with prevailing; after the treaty and the promise of clear victory, this ayah repeats “li-yuẓhirahu ʿalā al-dīni kullihi.” It places that prevailing purpose in the context of the Messenger's mission.

This ayah repeats the source section's root example, “li-yuẓhirahu ʿalā al-dīni kullihi,” and says the purpose stands despite the polytheists' dislike. It makes explicit the resistance against which the religion's prevailing is measured.

The source section's root note connects faraghta with becoming free of a task; here God says “sanafruġu lakum,” addressing humans and jinn before the challenge in 55:33. The speaker and direction reverse: human devotion after work becomes God's announced attention to his audience.

After Pharaoh threatens the newly believing magicians with mutilation and crucifixion, they ask “afriġ ʿalaynā ṣabran.” The same root-formula as 2:250 pours patience over people facing lethal violence, extending the source section's struggle image beyond battlefield combat.

The next ayah after the rule of retribution says “wa-lakum fī al-qiṣāṣi ḥayāh,” that life is preserved through it. It supplies the stated purpose of the blood-claim boundary in 2:178, rather than treating spilled blood as void.

The same prophetic address commands “wa-udhkur isma rabbika wa-tabattal ilayhi tabtīlā,” remembering the Lord and devoting oneself wholly to Him. This gives a close parallel to the source section's direction after the task: turn the renewed effort toward the Lord.

The Prophet is told that he has a long occupation by day; 73:8 then directs him to remember and devote himself to his Lord. Together they make explicit a rhythm of completing worldly work and turning to devotion, as in the source section's reading of faraghta then fanṣab.

The command “qumi al-layla” tells the wrapped Prophet to stand in prayer at night. It offers a concrete devotional form of the source section's fanṣab, whose stance is directed by the following “wa-ilā rabbika.”

God says “qawlan thaqīlā,” a weighty word will be cast upon the Prophet. The image of revelation as a weight borne by the same prophetic addressee gives a non-weapon parallel to the source section's burden on the back.

“Qum fa-andhir” commands the Prophet to rise and warn. This is a specific prophetic command to stand into further work, paralleling the source section's interpretation of fanṣab after one task is finished.

After commands to rise, warn, and purify, this ayah says “wa-li-rabbika faṣbir,” for your Lord be patient. Its explicit direction to the Lord parallels the source section's final turn away from an opponent and toward God.

“Those who strive in Us” are promised guidance to God's ways. This states the direction implicit in the source section's fanṣab followed by “wa-ilā rabbika”: effort is reoriented toward God, and that effort leads to His ways.

Believers are told to prepare whatever strength they can, including warhorses, to deter an enemy. This is the arming phase opposite to the source section's scene of putting battle gear down once war is over.

The mobilization command says “infirū khifāfan wa-thiqālan.” The phrase can mean light and heavy in more than one way, but in its war setting it suggests going out under differing loads, the opposite phase from the source section's gear being laid down.

The source section's root note identifies ẓahr as the back bearing a burden; 43:13 uses “ʿalā ẓuhūrihi” for the backs of riding animals, then tells riders to remember God's favor. The shared load-bearing body part is clear, though the contrast between strain and transport is interpretive.

God says He will make Jesus' followers prevail over those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. This is another specific formulation of the source section's dictionary sense of ẓ-h-r as religious dominance, with a different prophetic community and a stated duration.

After the battle at Uhud, this ayah tells believers not to lose heart or grieve and promises they will be uppermost if they remain believers. It gives a battle-context formulation of prevailing after a setback, alongside the source section's victory sense.

This ayah says that if a wound has touched the believers, a similar wound has touched the opposing people, and that God rotates such days among people. It concretely connects to the source section's dictionary image of a blow that spills blood, while showing battle wounds and fortunes as reciprocal and changing.

At Badr, God sends rain to purify the believers, strengthen their hearts, and make their feet firm. This parallels the battle prayer in 2:250 for patience and firm footing, showing divine support that lets fighters stand under pressure.

This ayah says that those who mislead will carry their own burdens fully and some burdens of those they misled on the Day of Resurrection. The source section's dictionary note uses wizr for war gear carried and laid down; this same root becomes a moral load that accumulates instead of being removed.

The verse says that the misleaders will carry their own burdens and additional burdens with them. The source section's dictionary root wizr evokes gear borne in battle and then set aside; here the burden in its moral sense is added and carried forward.

The verse promises that God will bring ease after hardship. This matches the specific sequence the source section develops: the war's weight is borne through struggle, then the burden is set down as the conflict ends.

This command tells believers to stand devoutly before God in prayer. It is a precise devotional counterpart to the source section's standing after finishing work and its immediate direction toward the Lord.

Addressed to the Prophet, this ayah commands patience for the Lord's judgment and glorification of the Lord when he rises. It closely joins the source section's two steps: stand after the task, then direct the stance to God.

The passage says that God's party will prevail. This is a further nonlexical formulation of the section's dictionary note that ẓ-h-r can mean prevailing, here cast as the outcome of the messengers' conflict with their deniers.

After recalling the abundance given to the Prophet, this ayah commands him to pray and sacrifice for his Lord. It offers a concrete act of renewed service directed to God, paralleling the source section's movement from completed labor to turning toward the Lord.

This ayah praises believers who fight in God's cause in aligned ranks, like a joined structure. It shows the organized battle-facing stance that the source section distinguishes from its post-task stance directed toward the Lord.
